topics.name: Blood
topics.kicker: The fluid the heart pumps · Carries oxygen, nutrients, and wastes
topics.dates: About 5 liters in an adult human body
topics.briefing: An adult carries about 5 liters of blood, and the heart pumps all of it around the body about once a minute. Just over half of it is a straw-colored liquid called plasma; the rest is red cells that carry oxygen, white cells that fight germs, and tiny platelets that plug leaks. Its red color comes from hemoglobin, an iron-rich protein, and despite the myth, it is never blue.
topics.answerHtml: Blood (accept whole blood; do not accept “plasma” or a single kind of blood cell)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Horseshoe crabs have a blue version of this substance, colored by a copper-containing protein called hemocyanin, and an extract of it is used to test medicines for bacterial toxins. In Antarctic icefish, this substance is nearly colorless because it has no hemoglobin at all.
tossups.r: In humans, it is a mix of plasma, platelets, and red and white cells. For 10 points, name this fluid that the heart pumps through arteries and veins.

tossups.p: In 1901, Karl Landsteiner found that samples of this fluid from different people can clump together when mixed, so he sorted it into groups he called A, B, and C. His group C was later renamed O.
tossups.r: The Rh factor, another way of grouping this fluid, is named for rhesus monkeys. For 10 points, name this fluid whose types include A, B, AB, and O.

tossups.p: William Harvey’s 1628 book _De Motu Cordis_ showed that this fluid travels around the body in a loop, rather than being constantly made by the liver and used up. In 1661, Marcello Malpighi [“mal-PEE-ghee”] found the tiny capillaries that connect the vessels carrying it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fluid carried away from the heart by arteries and back to it by veins.

tossups.p: Albumin, a protein made by the liver, is the most common protein in the liquid part of this substance. The clear, yellowish fluid that is left after this substance clots is called serum.
tossups.r: That liquid part, plasma, makes up about 55 percent of its volume. For 10 points, name this red fluid pumped by the heart.

tossups.p: A buffer made of carbonic acid and bicarbonate keeps the pH of this fluid between about 7.35 and 7.45, slightly basic. If that pH falls too low, a person develops acidosis.
tossups.r: Biologists classify this fluid as a connective tissue. For 10 points, name this substance made of plasma, platelets, and red and white cells.

tossups.p: When a sample of this fluid is spun in a centrifuge, a thin, pale layer called the buffy coat forms between the two main layers. The percentage of the sample taken up by the heavy bottom layer is called the hematocrit [“hih-MAT-uh-krit”].
tossups.r: That bottom layer is made of red cells, and the top layer is plasma. For 10 points, name this fluid pumped by the heart.

tossups.p: In ancient Greek medicine, this fluid was one of the four humors, and people thought to have extra of it were called “sanguine.” For centuries, doctors drained some of it from sick patients, sometimes using leeches, to try to balance the humors.
tossups.r: Modern donors give about a pint of it at a time for transfusions. For 10 points, name this red body fluid.

tossups.p: Medicinal leeches release a substance called hirudin [“hih-ROO-din”] that keeps this fluid from clotting while they feed. Doctors use medicines with a similar effect, such as heparin and warfarin, to prevent dangerous clots.
tossups.r: In humans, platelets and threads of a protein called fibrin help this fluid clot. For 10 points, name this fluid that the heart pumps.

tossups.p: Surgeon Charles Drew developed ways to separate and store the plasma from this fluid, and in 1940 he helped lead a program that shipped that plasma to Britain during World War II. Drew then directed an early American Red Cross bank that stored donations of this fluid.
tossups.r: Donors are often told their type, such as A, B, AB, or O. For 10 points, name this fluid collected at donation drives.

tossups.p: In the 1200s, the Arab physician Ibn al-Nafis correctly described how this fluid travels from the right side of the heart through the lungs to the left side, rather than passing through tiny pores in the heart’s wall. That route is called pulmonary circulation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fluid that picks up oxygen in the lungs and is pumped around the body by the heart.

tossups.p: Hematopoietic [“hee-muh-toh-poy-ET-ik”] stem cells in red bone marrow make every type of cell found in this fluid. The kidneys release a hormone called erythropoietin to tell the marrow to make more of its oxygen-carrying cells.
tossups.r: Those cells are packed with hemoglobin. For 10 points, name this red fluid that the heart pumps through the body.

tossups.p: Mixing two mismatched samples of this fluid makes its cells clump together, a reaction called agglutination [“uh-gloo-tih-NAY-shun”]. Because their red cells lack A, B, and Rh antigens, people with type O-negative are called “universal donors.”
tossups.r: Patients with type AB-positive are “universal recipients.” For 10 points, name this fluid that hospitals give in transfusions.

tossups.p: In the brain, tightly sealed capillary walls form a barrier that keeps many substances in this fluid away from nerve cells. A sphygmomanometer [“sfig-moh-muh-NOM-ih-ter”] measures the pressure of this fluid as two numbers, systolic over diastolic, in millimeters of mercury.
tossups.r: Arteries carry it away from the heart. For 10 points, name this fluid whose red cells carry oxygen around the body.

tossups.p: The Greek-based prefix “hemo-” and the Latin word “sanguis” both refer to this substance, which is studied by doctors called hematologists. Phlebotomists [“fleh-BOT-uh-mists”] are trained to collect samples of it, usually from a vein in the arm.
tossups.r: Its red color comes from the iron-containing protein hemoglobin. For 10 points, name this fluid pumped by the heart.

tossups.p: People with hemophilia, an inherited disorder that ran in Queen Victoria’s family, have trouble getting this fluid to clot. Normally, platelets gather at a cut while a protein called fibrinogen is turned into sticky threads of fibrin.
tossups.r: Despite a common myth, it is never blue in humans. For 10 points, name this red fluid that an adult has about 5 liters of.

clues.t: A red fluid pumped by the heart through arteries, veins, and capillaries
Made of liquid plasma plus red cells, white cells, and platelets
Carries oxygen and nutrients to the body’s cells and carries away carbon dioxide and wastes
Gets its red color from hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein in its red cells
Comes in types A, B, AB, and O, each Rh-positive or Rh-negative (Rh is named for rhesus monkeys)
Plasma, its straw-colored liquid part, is about 55 percent of its volume and mostly water
Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO groups in 1901; his group “C” was later renamed O
William Harvey’s _De Motu Cordis_ (1628) showed that it circulates in a loop pumped by the heart
All of its cells come from stem cells in red bone marrow, a process called hematopoiesis
Platelets and threads of fibrin (made from fibrinogen) make it clot; people with hemophilia clot poorly
Type O-negative donors are “universal donors”; type AB-positive patients are “universal recipients”
Classified as a connective tissue; an adult has about 5 liters of it
Never blue in humans, despite the myth; veins only look bluish through the skin
A carbonic acid and bicarbonate buffer keeps its pH between about 7.35 and 7.45; too low a pH is acidosis
Hematocrit: the percentage of its volume made of red cells, found by spinning a sample in a centrifuge
In a spun sample, white cells and platelets form a thin middle layer called the buffy coat
Albumin, made by the liver, is the most common protein in its plasma; serum is the fluid left after it clots
Marcello Malpighi found capillaries in 1661, completing Harvey’s picture of its circulation
Ibn al-Nafis described its path from the heart through the lungs (pulmonary circulation) in the 1200s
One of the four humors of ancient Greek medicine; people thought to have extra were called “sanguine”
Horseshoe crabs have a blue version colored by copper-based hemocyanin; an extract of it tests medicines for bacterial toxins
Antarctic icefish have a nearly colorless version with no hemoglobin
Hirudin (from leeches) and medicines such as heparin and warfarin keep it from clotting
Charles Drew found ways to store its plasma, helped lead a 1940 program shipping plasma to Britain, and directed an early Red Cross bank for it
Tightly sealed capillary walls form a barrier between it and the brain’s nerve cells
Its pressure is measured with a sphygmomanometer as systolic over diastolic, in millimeters of mercury
The prefix “hemo-” and the Latin “sanguis” refer to it; phlebotomists collect it and hematologists study it

trap.title: The whole, or a part?
trap.body: Tossups on this fluid are packed with clues about its parts: plasma, platelets, hemoglobin, red cells, and white cells. Nervous players buzz with the part they just heard instead of the whole fluid. Each of those parts is a separate answer line on this site (Red blood cells, White blood cells, Platelets, Hemoglobin, Blood types, Blood clotting), so naming one here is wrong.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun at the end. “This fluid,” “this tissue,” or “this substance pumped by the heart” means blood. Give a part only when the question asks for “these cells,” “this protein,” or “this liquid portion.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Blood (accept whole blood; do not accept “plasma” or a single kind of blood cell)

topics.name: Malaria
topics.kicker: Parasitic disease spread by mosquitoes · Named for Italian “bad air”
topics.dates: Parasite first seen by Alphonse Laveran in 1880
topics.briefing: Malaria is caused not by a virus or bacterium but by Plasmodium, a single-celled parasite carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Inside a person, the parasites multiply in the liver and then invade red blood cells, causing repeating waves of fever and chills. It is one of history’s deadliest diseases, but bed nets, the drug artemisinin, and the first vaccines, recommended in 2021 and 2023, are helping fight it.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The parasites that cause this disease digest hemoglobin inside red blood cells, leaving behind dark crystals of a pigment called hemozoin [“hee-moh-ZOH-in”]. The drug chloroquine was widely used against this disease until many of those parasites became resistant to it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by Plasmodium parasites and spread by the bites of Anopheles mosquitoes.

tossups.p: Two species that cause this disease, vivax and ovale, can hide in the liver as dormant forms called hypnozoites [“hip-noh-ZOH-ites”] and cause relapses weeks or months later. The drug primaquine is given to clear out those dormant liver forms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease spread by mosquitoes that causes repeating bouts of fever and chills.

tossups.p: In 1880, French army doctor Alphonse Laveran [“lav-RAHN”] became the first person to see the single-celled parasite behind this disease, in a patient’s blood. In 1897, Ronald Ross found that parasite in the stomach of a mosquito, a discovery remembered each August 20 on World Mosquito Day.
tossups.r: Both men won Nobel Prizes. For 10 points, name this disease caused by Plasmodium and carried by Anopheles mosquitoes.

tossups.p: Tu Youyou [“TOO yoh-YOH”] shared a 2015 Nobel Prize after a 4th-century Chinese medical text led her to a treatment for this disease made from sweet wormwood. That drug, artemisinin [“ar-teh-MISS-ih-nin”], is combined with other medicines to treat this disease around the world.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by Plasmodium parasites that spread through mosquito bites.

tossups.p: Jesuit missionaries helped bring a bark nicknamed “Jesuit’s bark” from Peru to Europe to treat this disease. In 1820, Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Caventou isolated the bark’s bitter active ingredient, which also flavors tonic water.
tossups.r: That ingredient is quinine, from the cinchona tree. For 10 points, name this disease spread by Anopheles mosquitoes.

tossups.p: Many people in West and Central Africa lack the Duffy antigen on their red blood cells, which helps protect them from vivax, one of the species that cause this disease, since vivax uses that antigen to enter the cells.
tossups.r: Insecticide-treated bed nets help prevent this disease. For 10 points, name this illness caused by Plasmodium parasites and spread by Anopheles mosquitoes.

tossups.p: In the classic example of heterozygote advantage, people who carry one copy of the gene for sickle-cell hemoglobin are partly protected from this disease. That protection helps explain why the sickle-cell gene is common in regions where this disease is widespread.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mosquito-borne disease caused by Plasmodium parasites that invade red blood cells.

tossups.p: The Communicable Disease Center, which became the CDC, was founded in Atlanta in 1946, growing out of a wartime office set up to fight this disease in the American South. By the early 1950s, this disease had been eliminated from the United States.
tossups.r: It causes repeating fevers and chills. For 10 points, name this disease spread by Anopheles mosquitoes and caused by Plasmodium.

tossups.p: In 2021, the World Health Organization recommended RTS,S, the first vaccine against this disease, and in 2023 it recommended a second vaccine, R21. This disease kills hundreds of thousands of people each year, most of them young children in Africa.
tossups.r: People in at-risk areas protect themselves with bed nets and insect repellent. For 10 points, name this disease carried by Anopheles mosquitoes.

tossups.p: During the building of the Panama Canal, William Gorgas cut cases of yellow fever and this other disease by draining standing water and spreading oil on ponds where mosquitoes bred. Buildings were also fitted with screens to keep out the mosquitoes that carry this disease.
tossups.r: Its name comes from Italian words meaning “bad air.” For 10 points, name this disease caused by Plasmodium parasites.

tossups.p: Paul Müller won a 1948 Nobel Prize for discovering that DDT kills insects, and DDT spraying was a key part of the World Health Organization’s 1955 campaign to wipe out this disease. That campaign worked in some countries, but mosquitoes became resistant to DDT.
tossups.r: Quinine was an early treatment for it. For 10 points, name this disease carried by Anopheles mosquitoes and caused by Plasmodium.

tossups.p: The deadliest species that causes this disease forms crescent-shaped cells called gametocytes, the stage that a feeding mosquito picks up. That species, falciparum, causes most deaths from this disease in Africa.
tossups.r: Infected red blood cells break open on a regular cycle, causing repeating fevers. For 10 points, name this disease caused by Plasmodium parasites.

tossups.p: Unlike many other mosquitoes, the ones that spread this disease rest at a steep angle with their abdomens pointed up, and their larvae lie flat against the water’s surface. Only the females of that genus, Anopheles [“uh-NOFF-uh-leez”], bite people.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by Plasmodium parasites and treated with drugs like quinine and artemisinin.

tossups.p: The parasites that cause this disease reproduce sexually inside mosquitoes, which makes the mosquito their definitive host. Forms called sporozoites [“SPOR-uh-ZOH-ites”] travel from the mosquito’s salivary glands to a person’s liver, where they multiply and release new forms that invade red blood cells.
tossups.r: Its main symptoms are repeating fevers and chills. For 10 points, name this disease caused by Plasmodium.

tossups.p: Plasmodium knowlesi [“NOHLZ-ee-eye”], which normally infects macaque monkeys, can also give people this disease in Southeast Asia. People once blamed this disease on foul air rising from swamps, which is why its name comes from the Italian for “bad air.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease spread by Anopheles mosquitoes and treated with quinine.

clues.t: Spread by the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes
Caused by single-celled parasites in the genus Plasmodium, not by a virus or bacterium
Its name comes from Italian for “bad air,” from an old belief that swamp air caused it
Long treated with quinine, from the bark of the South American cinchona tree
Causes repeating bouts of fever and chills
The parasites first multiply in the liver, then invade red blood cells
One copy of the sickle-cell gene gives partial protection against it, the classic case of heterozygote advantage
Plasmodium falciparum is the deadliest species and causes most deaths from it in Africa
Prevented with insecticide-treated bed nets and by draining standing water where mosquitoes breed
Ronald Ross found its parasite in a mosquito in 1897 (marked by World Mosquito Day, August 20) and won the 1902 Nobel Prize
French army doctor Alphonse Laveran first saw its parasite in a patient’s blood in 1880
Tu Youyou found the drug artemisinin in sweet wormwood and shared a 2015 Nobel Prize
Vivax and ovale can lie dormant in the liver as hypnozoites and cause relapses; primaquine clears them
The parasites digest hemoglobin and leave dark crystals of a pigment called hemozoin
Chloroquine was a standard drug against it until many parasites became resistant
People who lack the Duffy antigen on their red blood cells resist vivax, which uses that antigen to get in
The CDC began in Atlanta in 1946, growing out of a wartime office that fought it in the American South
William Gorgas fought it and yellow fever by controlling mosquitoes during the building of the Panama Canal
Paul Müller won a 1948 Nobel Prize for showing that DDT kills insects; DDT was central to the WHO’s 1955 campaign against it
The WHO recommended the first vaccines against it: RTS,S in 2021 and R21 in 2023
Its parasite reproduces sexually inside the mosquito, which makes the mosquito its definitive host
Sporozoites travel from a mosquito’s salivary glands to a person’s liver
Anopheles mosquitoes rest at a steep angle with abdomens raised, and their larvae lie flat on the water
Pelletier and Caventou isolated quinine in 1820; cinchona bark was nicknamed “Jesuit’s bark”
Falciparum’s gametocytes, the stage that a feeding mosquito picks up, are crescent-shaped
Plasmodium knowlesi, a parasite of macaque monkeys, also infects people in Southeast Asia

trap.title: Disease, parasite, or mosquito?
trap.body: These tossups describe three different things: the disease, the Plasmodium parasite that causes it, and the Anopheles mosquito that carries it. If the question asks for “this disease,” naming the parasite or the mosquito is wrong. Players also mix it up with other mosquito-borne diseases, such as yellow fever, dengue, and Zika, which are caused by viruses.
trap.fix: Plasmodium is the parasite, Anopheles is the mosquito, and malaria is the disease. Quinine, artemisinin, hypnozoites, and the sickle-cell trait point to malaria; Walter Reed and Aedes mosquitoes point to yellow fever.
trap.line: Real answer line: Malaria (do not accept “Plasmodium” or “mosquito”)

topics.name: Mitosis
topics.kicker: Cell division that splits the nucleus · Makes two identical daughter cells
topics.briefing: Your body makes millions of new cells every second, and they come from mitosis. In this kind of cell division, a cell that has already copied its chromosomes splits its nucleus so each new cell gets an identical, complete set, which is how you grow and how a scraped knee heals. It is usually taught as four stages, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase (“PMAT”), and then cytokinesis pinches the cell in two.
topics.answerHtml: Mitosis (accept karyokinesis or M phase; prompt on cell division; do not accept “meiosis” or the name of a single stage, such as “prophase”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Walther Flemming named this process in 1882 from the Greek word for “thread,” based on his studies of stained cells from salamanders. Flemming also coined the word chromatin for the material that coils up into visible chromosomes during this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this kind of cell division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells.

tossups.p: Colchicine [“KOL-chih-seen”] halts this process at metaphase by keeping spindle microtubules from forming, a trick used to prepare karyotypes. The cancer drug Taxol, first found in the bark of the Pacific yew, also stops this process by interfering with microtubules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that splits one nucleus into two identical nuclei.

tossups.p: In many fungi, including yeasts, this process is “closed” because the nuclear envelope never breaks apart. In animal cells, the envelope does break apart during a stage called prometaphase, so that spindle fibers can grab the chromosomes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this kind of nuclear division that keeps the chromosome number the same.

tossups.p: Most plant cells carry out this process without centrioles, the paired cylinders found in the centrosomes of animal cells. As this process ends, a structure called the phragmoplast [“FRAG-moh-plast”] guides vesicles from the Golgi apparatus that build a new cell plate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of cell division often observed in onion root tips.

tossups.p: The anaphase-promoting complex starts the separation stage of this process by freeing an enzyme called separase, which cuts the cohesin rings that hold sister chromatids together. The chromatids are then pulled to opposite ends of the cell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process whose stages include prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase.

tossups.p: Tim Hunt discovered proteins called cyclins, which rise and fall to control when cells begin this process, by studying sea urchin eggs. Hunt shared a 2001 Nobel Prize with Leland Hartwell and Paul Nurse for finding key regulators of the cell cycle.
tossups.r: It is followed by cytokinesis. For 10 points, name this process that divides one nucleus into two identical nuclei.

tossups.p: The spindle assembly checkpoint delays the start of anaphase in this process until every chromosome’s kinetochore [“kih-NET-oh-kor”] is attached to spindle fibers. Kinetochores are protein structures that form at each chromosome’s centromere.
tossups.r: During this process, chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate. For 10 points, name this process that produces two identical daughter cells.

tossups.p: Biology students often look for this process in slides of whitefish embryos and onion root tips, where cells divide quickly. In those slides, cells in its first stage show thick, condensed chromosomes and no visible nucleolus.
tossups.r: That stage is prophase. For 10 points, name this process of cell division whose stages also include metaphase and anaphase.

tossups.p: Leonard Hayflick found that normal human cells grown in a lab can go through this process only about 40 to 60 times before they stop. Each round of copying shortens the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes, called telomeres.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that splits a nucleus to make two identical body cells.

tossups.p: Most mature nerve cells stay in a resting stage called G0 and rarely, if ever, go through this process again. Most other cells spend far more time in interphase, which includes the S phase when DNA is copied, than in this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this part of the cell cycle that includes prophase and telophase.

tossups.p: Star-shaped clusters of microtubules called asters form around the centrosomes as this process begins in animal cells. During this process’s first stage, chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, the nucleolus fades away, and the centrosomes move toward opposite sides of the cell.
tossups.r: In its last stage, telophase, new nuclear envelopes form. For 10 points, name this process that produces two identical daughter cells.

tossups.p: In anaphase A of this process, kinetochore microtubules shorten and pull chromatids toward the poles, while in anaphase B the poles themselves move farther apart. Motor proteins such as kinesins and dynein help power these movements.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which a cell’s copied chromosomes are split evenly between two new nuclei.

tossups.p: As this process finishes, a contractile ring of actin and myosin forms a cleavage furrow that pinches an animal cell in two. That splitting of the cytoplasm, called cytokinesis, usually begins during this process’s final stage, telophase.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that, unlike meiosis, keeps the chromosome number the same.

tossups.p: Vinblastine and vincristine, drugs made from the Madagascar periwinkle, treat some cancers by blocking this process. Cancer cells go through this process again and again because the checkpoints that normally control the cell cycle no longer work properly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of cell division that makes two identical copies of a cell.

tossups.p: Rudolf Virchow popularized the idea that every cell comes from another cell, summed up in the Latin phrase “omnis cellula e cellula.” Bacteria divide by binary fission, but the body cells of plants and animals divide their nuclei by this process.
tossups.r: In human body cells, it makes two diploid cells, while meiosis makes four haploid ones. For 10 points, name this kind of cell division.

clues.t: Divides a cell’s nucleus to make two genetically identical daughter cells
Its stages, in order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (“PMAT”)
Lets the body grow and replace old or damaged cells
Unlike meiosis, it keeps the chromosome number the same (46 in human body cells)
Comes after interphase (G1, S, and G2), when the cell grows and copies its DNA; mature nerve cells rest in G0
Prophase: chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nucleolus disappears
Metaphase: chromosomes line up along the middle of the cell, called the metaphase plate
Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite ends of the cell
Telophase: new nuclear envelopes form around the two sets of chromosomes
Spindle fibers made of microtubules grow from centrosomes, ringed by star-shaped asters in animal cells
Usually followed by cytokinesis: a ring of actin and myosin pinches animal cells in two, while plant cells build a cell plate
Often observed in slides of onion root tips and whitefish embryos
Named in 1882 by Walther Flemming, from the Greek for “thread”; he studied salamander cells and coined “chromatin”
Spindle fibers attach to kinetochores, protein structures at each chromosome’s centromere
Prometaphase: the nuclear envelope breaks apart so microtubules can grab the chromosomes
The anaphase-promoting complex frees separase, which cuts the cohesin holding sister chromatids together
Anaphase A pulls chromatids to the poles; in anaphase B, the poles themselves move farther apart
Timed by cyclins and kinases; Hartwell, Hunt (who found cyclins in sea urchin eggs), and Nurse shared the 2001 Nobel Prize
The spindle assembly checkpoint holds off anaphase until every kinetochore is attached
Colchicine blocks spindle formation and stops cells at metaphase, which helps in making karyotypes
Cancer drugs Taxol (from the Pacific yew) and vinblastine (from the Madagascar periwinkle) block it
In many fungi, including yeasts, it is “closed”: the nuclear envelope never breaks down
Most plant cells do it without centrioles; as it ends, a phragmoplast builds the cell plate from Golgi vesicles
Hayflick limit: normal human cells can divide only about 40 to 60 times as their telomeres shorten
Rudolf Virchow popularized “omnis cellula e cellula”: every cell comes from another cell

trap.title: Whole process, or one stage?
trap.body: Mitosis and meiosis sound alike and share stage names (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase), so one wrong vowel costs the tossup. Many tossups also spend their power clues on a single stage, which tempts players to buzz with “anaphase” or “prophase” when the question wants the whole process. Cytokinesis, the splitting of the cytoplasm, is a separate step that usually follows it.
trap.fix: Two identical cells, growth, repair, or onion root tips mean mitosis; four haploid cells, gametes, crossing over, or tetrads mean meiosis. If the question says “this process” or “this kind of cell division,” never answer with a stage name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mitosis (accept karyokinesis or M phase; prompt on cell division; do not accept “meiosis” or the name of a single stage)

topics.name: Enzymes
topics.kicker: Protein catalysts of living cells · Names usually end in “-ase”
topics.briefing: Drop fresh pineapple into gelatin and it will never set, because the fruit contains an enzyme that chops up proteins. Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up reactions by lowering the energy needed to start them, and they come out unchanged, ready to work again. Each has an active site shaped to fit its target, which is why heat that bends that shape can “denature” it.
topics.answerHtml: Enzymes (accept enzyme; prompt on catalysts or proteins; do not accept “coenzymes” or “substrates”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Alexander Fleming discovered one of these molecules, lysozyme, which is found in tears and breaks down the cell walls of some bacteria. In 1965, lysozyme became the first of these molecules to have its three-dimensional structure worked out by X-ray crystallography.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these biological catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering activation energy.

tossups.p: James Sumner crystallized urease from jack beans in 1926, helping prove that these substances are proteins, though many scientists doubted him at first. He shared a 1946 Nobel Prize with John Northrop, who crystallized the stomach protein pepsin.
tossups.r: Most of these substances have names ending in “-ase.” For 10 points, name these biological catalysts.

tossups.p: Eduard Buchner won a 1907 Nobel Prize for showing that juice squeezed from ground-up yeast cells could still ferment sugar, proving that fermentation did not require living cells. Buchner named the active substance in that juice zymase [“ZYE-mayss”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these protein catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in living things.

tossups.p: In 1833, Anselme Payen [“pah-YAN”] discovered diastase, a starch-digesting substance from malt that was the first of these molecules ever found. Wilhelm Kühne [“KOO-nuh”] later named these molecules from Greek words meaning “in yeast.”
tossups.r: Amylase, which starts digesting starch in human saliva, is one of them. For 10 points, name these biological catalysts, which are usually proteins.

tossups.p: A Lineweaver–Burk plot uses reciprocals to turn rate data for these molecules into a straight line. That data is often modeled with an equation published in 1913 by Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten, which includes a constant called Km.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these biological catalysts, which are often proteins whose names end in “-ase.”

tossups.p: Aspirin works by permanently blocking cyclooxygenase [“sye-kloh-OK-sih-jen-ayss”], one of these molecules. Competitive inhibitors slow down these molecules by blocking their active sites, while noncompetitive inhibitors attach somewhere else and change their shape.
tossups.r: Adding more substrate can overcome only the competitive kind. For 10 points, name these biological catalysts that lower activation energy.

tossups.p: Thomas Cech [“CHEK”] and Sidney Altman won the 1989 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering RNA molecules that act as these substances, called ribozymes. The ribosome itself uses RNA in this role when it links amino acids together.
tossups.r: Most of these substances, however, are proteins. For 10 points, name these biological catalysts.

tossups.p: Taq polymerase, one of these substances that can survive near-boiling temperatures, comes from a bacterium first found in a hot spring in Yellowstone National Park. Taq polymerase is used to copy DNA in a technique called PCR.
tossups.r: Helicase and DNA ligase are other examples. For 10 points, name these protein catalysts.

tossups.p: Fresh pineapple keeps gelatin desserts from setting because it contains bromelain [“BROH-muh-lin”], one of these substances that breaks down proteins. Papain [“puh-PAY-in”], a similar substance from papaya, is used in powdered meat tenderizers.
tossups.r: Heating pineapple, as in canning, inactivates bromelain by changing its shape. For 10 points, name these protein catalysts that heat can denature.

tossups.p: Catalase, one of these molecules, splits hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen so quickly that a slice of raw potato or liver makes peroxide fizz. Catalase has one of the highest turnover numbers known, handling millions of molecules every second.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these biological catalysts that work by lowering activation energy without being used up.

tossups.p: Some of these molecules are made as inactive forms called zymogens [“ZYE-muh-jinz”], such as pepsinogen, which stomach acid turns into pepsin. In the small intestine, trypsinogen is switched on by enteropeptidase to become trypsin.
tossups.r: Pepsin and trypsin both break down proteins. For 10 points, name these biological catalysts, which include many digestive proteins.

tossups.p: Carbonic anhydrase, one of these molecules found in red blood cells, needs a zinc ion at its active site to work. Many others rely on organic helper molecules such as NAD+, which the body makes from the vitamin niacin.
tossups.r: Metal ions that help them are called cofactors. For 10 points, name these biological catalysts, which are usually proteins.

tossups.p: Daniel Koshland’s induced-fit model says these molecules change shape slightly when they grab their targets, improving on Emil Fischer’s 1894 “lock and key” model. In both models, a reactant called the substrate fits into an active site.
tossups.r: RuBisCo, which grabs carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, is one of them. For 10 points, name these biological catalysts.

tossups.p: In feedback inhibition, the end product of a pathway shuts down one of these molecules early in the pathway by binding to its allosteric site. Pepsin, one of these molecules in the stomach, works best at an acidic pH of about 2.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these biological catalysts that can be denatured by too much heat.

tossups.p: Frances Arnold shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using “directed evolution” to create new and better versions of these molecules. Laundry detergents labeled “bio” contain these molecules to break down stains made of protein, fat, and starch.
tossups.r: Lactase, which breaks down the sugar in milk, is one of them. For 10 points, name these biological catalysts, whose names often end in “-ase.”

clues.t: Biological catalysts, usually proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in living things
Work by lowering a reaction’s activation energy, without being used up
Names usually end in “-ase,” as in lactase, amylase, and lipase
The molecule each one acts on, the substrate, fits into a pocket called the active site
Too much heat or the wrong pH can denature them, changing their shape so they stop working
Emil Fischer’s lock-and-key model (1894) and Daniel Koshland’s induced-fit model (1958) describe how they grab substrates
Competitive inhibitors block the active site; noncompetitive inhibitors bind somewhere else and change the shape
Many need helpers: metal-ion cofactors such as zinc, or vitamin-based molecules such as NAD+ (made from niacin)
Each works best at an optimal temperature and pH; stomach pepsin works best near pH 2
Digestive examples: amylase breaks down starch, trypsin breaks down proteins, and lipase breaks down fats
Catalase splits hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, making peroxide fizz on raw potato or liver
Their rates follow Michaelis–Menten kinetics (1913); Km is the substrate level that gives half the top speed
A Lineweaver–Burk (double-reciprocal) plot turns their rate data into a straight line
James Sumner crystallized urease from jack beans in 1926, helping prove these are proteins (1946 Nobel Prize)
Eduard Buchner showed in 1897 that juice from ground-up yeast could still ferment sugar; he named its active substance zymase
Anselme Payen discovered the first one, diastase (from malt), in 1833
Wilhelm Kühne named them from Greek words meaning “in yeast”
Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman won the 1989 Nobel Prize for finding ribozymes, RNA molecules that do the same job
Alexander Fleming found lysozyme, which is in tears; in 1965 it became the first one whose structure was solved by X-ray crystallography
Taq polymerase, from a bacterium found in a Yellowstone hot spring, survives the heat of PCR
Bromelain in fresh pineapple keeps gelatin from setting; papain from papaya tenderizes meat
Some are made as inactive zymogens: pepsinogen becomes pepsin, and trypsinogen becomes trypsin
Feedback inhibition: a pathway’s end product shuts down an early step by binding an allosteric site
RuBisCo, which fixes carbon dioxide in photosynthesis, is often called the most abundant one on Earth
Frances Arnold shared the 2018 Chemistry Nobel for “directed evolution” of new versions; “bio” detergents use them on stains

trap.title: Catalyst, helper, or target?
trap.body: Enzymes are biological catalysts, so “catalysts” is close but earns only a prompt: say the more specific word. Players also mix up the enzyme with the molecule it works on (the substrate) and with its helpers (cofactors and vitamin-based coenzymes). Not every enzyme is a protein, since RNA ribozymes do the same job, which is why “proteins” is only a prompt too.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these biological catalysts” or “these proteins whose names end in -ase,” or mentions active sites and activation energy, say enzymes. If it asks for the thing that fits into the active site, that is the substrate.
trap.line: Real answer line: Enzymes (accept enzyme; prompt on catalysts or proteins; do not accept “coenzymes” or “substrates”)

topics.name: Red blood cells
topics.kicker: Disc-shaped oxygen carriers · Packed with hemoglobin, no nucleus
topics.briefing: A single drop of blood holds millions of red blood cells, and they are the most common cells in your body. These tiny, dented discs have no nucleus, which leaves more room for hemoglobin, the iron-rich protein that grabs oxygen in the lungs and gives blood its red color. Each one squeezes through narrow capillaries for about 120 days before the spleen or liver recycles it.
topics.answerHtml: Red blood cells (accept erythrocytes, RBCs, or red corpuscles; prompt on blood cells or blood; do not accept “white blood cells” or “hemoglobin”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Jan Swammerdam is usually credited as the first person to describe these cells, which he saw in frog blood through an early microscope in 1658. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek [“LAY-vun-hook”] described and measured these cells more precisely in the 1670s.
tossups.r: These cells get their color from hemoglobin. For 10 points, name these oxygen-carrying blood cells.

tossups.p: Camels and llamas are unusual among mammals because these cells in their blood are oval instead of round. In birds, reptiles, and fish, these cells keep their nucleus, but in mammals they push it out as they mature.
tossups.r: These cells are made in red bone marrow. For 10 points, name these disc-shaped cells that carry oxygen using hemoglobin.

tossups.p: Young versions of these cells, called reticulocytes [“reh-TIK-yoo-loh-sites”], still hold leftover RNA that shows up as a net-like mesh when stained. Athletes who train at high altitudes can end up with more of these cells, because low oxygen levels make the kidneys release the hormone erythropoietin [“ih-RITH-roh-POY-ih-tin”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these blood cells that carry oxygen to the body’s tissues.

tossups.p: Breaking down the hemoglobin from these cells produces bilirubin, a yellow pigment that can build up and cause jaundice. In the spleen, an organ nicknamed these cells’ “graveyard,” large white blood cells remove old ones from circulation.
tossups.r: Each of these cells lives about 120 days. For 10 points, name these oxygen-carrying blood cells.

tossups.p: In the chloride shift, these cells trade bicarbonate ions to the plasma in exchange for chloride ions. Inside these cells, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase turns carbon dioxide and water into carbonic acid.
tossups.r: These cells also carry some carbon dioxide back to the lungs. For 10 points, name these blood cells that carry oxygen using hemoglobin.

tossups.p: A molecule called 2,3-BPG, made inside these cells, helps them unload oxygen in the body’s tissues. They also give up more oxygen in acidic, carbon dioxide–rich areas, thanks to the Bohr effect, named for Niels Bohr’s father, Christian.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these hemoglobin-filled blood cells that are made in bone marrow.

tossups.p: In 1925, Gorter and Grendel extracted the fats from the membranes of these cells and found enough to cover their surface twice, which led to the idea of the lipid bilayer. The empty membranes left after these cells burst are called “ghosts.”
tossups.r: In mammals, these cells have no nucleus. For 10 points, name these oxygen-carrying cells, which get their color from hemoglobin.

tossups.p: Peter Agre shared a 2003 Nobel Prize for discovering aquaporins, channels that let water rush across cell membranes, in the membranes of these cells. Placed in pure water, these cells swell up and burst, which is called hemolysis.
tossups.r: In very salty water, they shrivel instead. For 10 points, name these cells that carry oxygen through the body.

tossups.p: In 1949, Linus Pauling’s team called a disorder affecting these cells a “molecular disease,” and Vernon Ingram later traced it to a single amino acid change in hemoglobin. In that disorder, sickle-cell disease, these cells can bend into stiff crescent shapes.
tossups.r: Normally, these cells are flexible, biconcave discs. For 10 points, name these oxygen-carrying cells found in blood.

tossups.p: A mesh of the protein spectrin just under the membrane of these cells lets them bend through narrow capillaries and spring back into shape. In hereditary spherocytosis [“sfeer-oh-sye-TOH-sis”], faulty membrane proteins make these cells spherical instead of their usual biconcave disc shape.
tossups.r: These cells are the most common cells in the human body. For 10 points, name these hemoglobin-packed cells that carry oxygen.

tossups.p: These cells can stack up like piles of coins in formations called rouleaux [“roo-LOH”]. When a blood sample is spun in a centrifuge, these cells sink to the bottom, and the percentage of the sample they fill is called the hematocrit.
tossups.r: Each one lives about four months. For 10 points, name these blood cells that use hemoglobin to carry oxygen.

tossups.p: The A1C test for diabetes measures how much sugar has stuck to the hemoglobin inside these cells, which shows a person’s average blood sugar over the past two to three months. That works because each of these cells lasts about 120 days.
tossups.r: In mammals, they lose their nucleus as they mature. For 10 points, name these oxygen-carrying cells made in bone marrow.

tossups.p: Because they lack mitochondria, these cells make all of their ATP by glycolysis and do not use the oxygen they carry to make energy. They also lack a nucleus, which leaves extra room for the hemoglobin packed inside them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these biconcave cells, the most common cells in the human body.

tossups.p: Plasmodium parasites spend part of their life cycle inside these cells, which break open on a regular schedule and cause the repeating fevers of malaria. People who carry one copy of the sickle-cell gene, which changes the hemoglobin inside these cells, have some protection against malaria.
tossups.r: These cells are shaped like discs dented in on both sides. For 10 points, name these oxygen-carrying blood cells.

tossups.p: Because they are about 7 to 8 micrometers across, these cells are often used as a built-in ruler for judging the size of other things on microscope slides. Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds to the hemoglobin in these cells far more tightly than oxygen does.
tossups.r: Antigens on these cells decide whether a person’s blood type is A, B, AB, or O. For 10 points, name these oxygen-carrying cells.

clues.t: Carry oxygen from the lungs to the body’s tissues
Packed with hemoglobin, the iron-containing protein that makes them red
Shaped like flexible discs dented in on both sides (biconcave)
In mammals, mature ones have no nucleus
The most common type of cell in the human body
Made in red bone marrow; the kidney hormone erythropoietin (EPO) speeds up production, as at high altitude
Each one lives about 120 days
Old ones are removed by the spleen, nicknamed their “graveyard,” and by the liver
Antigens on their surface set a person’s ABO blood type and Rh factor
Hematocrit: the percentage of blood volume they fill, measured by spinning blood in a centrifuge
In pure water they swell and burst (hemolysis); in very salty water they shrivel
Sickle-cell disease, caused by a single amino acid change in hemoglobin, can bend them into crescent shapes
Lacking mitochondria, they make ATP only by glycolysis
Malaria parasites (Plasmodium) multiply inside them
Jan Swammerdam first described them, in frog blood, in 1658; Antonie van Leeuwenhoek measured them in the 1670s
Camels and llamas have oval ones; birds, reptiles, and fish have ones with nuclei
Young ones, called reticulocytes, still hold leftover RNA that looks like a net when stained
Breaking down their hemoglobin makes yellow bilirubin, which builds up in jaundice
Carbonic anhydrase inside them turns carbon dioxide into carbonic acid; in the chloride shift, they trade bicarbonate for chloride
2,3-BPG made inside them helps hemoglobin release oxygen in the tissues
Bohr effect: acid and carbon dioxide make their hemoglobin give up oxygen; named for Christian Bohr, Niels Bohr’s father
In 1925, Gorter and Grendel used their membranes to propose the lipid bilayer; their empty membranes are called “ghosts”
Peter Agre found aquaporin water channels in their membranes, sharing a 2003 Nobel Prize
Linus Pauling’s team called sickle-cell anemia a “molecular disease” in 1949; Vernon Ingram found the amino acid change
A mesh of spectrin under their membrane keeps them flexible; faulty proteins make them spherical in hereditary spherocytosis
They can stack like piles of coins in formations called rouleaux
The A1C test for diabetes measures sugar stuck to their hemoglobin over the past two to three months
About 7 to 8 micrometers across, they serve as a built-in ruler on microscope slides

trap.title: Cell, protein, or fluid?
trap.body: Tossups on these cells talk constantly about hemoglobin, so players buzz with “hemoglobin,” which is the protein inside the cells, not the cells themselves. Others say “blood,” which is only a prompt here, or mix them up with white blood cells, which fight infection, and platelets, which help clotting.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these cells” that carry oxygen, lack a nucleus, or live about 120 days, say red blood cells (or erythrocytes). Say hemoglobin only for “this protein,” and white blood cells for clues about antibodies, phagocytes, or lymphocytes.
trap.line: Real answer line: Red blood cells (accept erythrocytes, RBCs, or red corpuscles; prompt on blood cells or blood; do not accept “white blood cells” or “hemoglobin”)

topics.name: Skin
topics.kicker: The body’s largest organ · A waterproof, germ-blocking shield
topics.dates: The largest organ of the human body
topics.briefing: Your skin is your largest organ, and you are constantly shedding its outer cells and growing new ones to replace them. Its outer layer, the epidermis, is a waterproof shield topped with tough, dead cells full of keratin, while the dermis beneath holds sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles. It also makes vitamin D in sunlight and gets its color from a pigment called melanin.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Surgeons try to cut along Langer’s lines, which follow the direction of the collagen fibers in this organ, so that cuts heal with smaller scars. The deeper of this organ’s two main layers, the dermis, holds blood vessels, nerves, and hair follicles.
tossups.r: Its outer layer, the epidermis, contains the pigment melanin. For 10 points, name this largest organ of the human body.

tossups.p: Lungless salamanders take in all of their oxygen through the lining of their mouths and through this organ, which must stay moist to work. Snakes shed the outer layer of this organ, often in one piece, in a process called ecdysis [“EK-dih-sis”].
tossups.r: In humans, it is the body’s largest organ. For 10 points, name this organ whose layers include the epidermis.

tossups.p: A mnemonic for the layers in the outer part of this organ is “Come, Let’s Get Sun Burned,” for the strata corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, and basale. The stratum lucidum shows up only in the thick parts of this organ on the palms and soles.
tossups.r: Sweat glands and hair follicles sit in its deeper layer, the dermis. For 10 points, name this organ whose outer layer is the epidermis.

tossups.p: Langerhans [“LAHNG-er-hahns”] cells in this organ’s outer layer act as lookouts for the immune system, while Merkel cells near the base of that layer help sense light touch. That outer layer, the epidermis, has no blood vessels of its own.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ, the body’s largest, which protects against germs and water loss.

tossups.p: Onion-like Pacinian [“puh-SIN-ee-un”] corpuscles deep in this organ sense pressure and vibration, while Meissner’s [“MYSE-nerz”] corpuscles near its surface sense light touch. Ruffini endings in it respond to stretching, and free nerve endings in it detect pain, heat, and cold.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that covers the body and gives people their sense of touch.

tossups.p: When ultraviolet B light strikes this organ, a molecule in it called 7-dehydrocholesterol is turned into vitamin D3. Too much ultraviolet light can cause sunburn and damage the DNA in this organ’s cells.
tossups.r: Its outer layer is called the epidermis. For 10 points, name this organ, whose color comes mainly from the pigment melanin.

tossups.p: Brown-black eumelanin [“yoo-MEL-uh-nin”] and red-yellow pheomelanin [“fee-oh-MEL-uh-nin”] help give this organ its color. People with darker or lighter coloring have about the same number of melanocytes, the pigment-making cells in this organ, but those cells make different amounts of pigment.
tossups.r: People with albinism make little or no melanin. For 10 points, name this organ, whose outer layer is called the epidermis.

tossups.p: Eccrine [“EK-rin”] glands cover most of this organ and release watery sweat that cools the body, while apocrine glands open into hair follicles in places like the armpits. Sebaceous [“sih-BAY-shus”] glands in this organ release an oily substance called sebum.
tossups.r: Its outer layer is the epidermis. For 10 points, name this organ, the largest in the human body.

tossups.p: Tiny muscles called arrector pili [“uh-REK-ter PYE-lye”] attach to hair follicles in this organ and cause goosebumps when they contract. When the body overheats, vessels in this organ widen to release heat, which can make a person look flushed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ made up of the epidermis and the dermis.

tossups.p: A polar bear’s fur looks white, but this organ underneath it is black. In humans, the outermost layer of this organ, the stratum corneum, is made of flat, dead cells filled with the tough protein keratin.
tossups.r: Hair and nails grow from this organ. For 10 points, name this organ that covers the outside of the body.

tossups.p: Doctors use the “rule of nines” to estimate how much of this organ has been damaged by a burn. A first-degree burn, like a typical sunburn, affects only this organ’s outer layer, the epidermis.
tossups.r: Its deeper layer, the dermis, holds sweat glands and hair follicles. For 10 points, name this organ, the largest in the body.

tossups.p: Francis Galton sorted the ridge patterns that this organ forms on the fingertips into arches, loops, and whorls. Koalas have ridge patterns on their fingers so similar to human ones that they can be hard to tell apart.
tossups.r: Those patterns are fingerprints. For 10 points, name this organ that covers the human body.

tossups.p: New keratinocytes [“keh-RAT-in-oh-sites”] form in the stratum basale at the bottom of this organ’s outer layer, then move upward as they fill with a tough protein and die. Those dead cells are constantly shed from the surface of this organ.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ whose outer layer is the epidermis and whose inner layer is the dermis.

tossups.p: The Greek word “derma” and the Latin word “cutis” both name this organ, which is why a shot given just beneath it is called “subcutaneous.” Doctors called dermatologists specialize in treating it.
tossups.r: It gets its color from melanin and makes vitamin D in sunlight. For 10 points, name this largest organ of the human body.

tossups.p: Collagen and elastin fibers give this organ’s dermis its strength and stretch, and as those fibers break down with age, wrinkles form. The unbroken surface of this organ is the body’s first line of defense against germs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that covers the outside of the human body and is its largest organ.

clues.t: The largest organ of the human body
Two main layers: the outer epidermis and the inner dermis, with a fatty layer below
Gets its color mainly from the pigment melanin
A waterproof barrier and the body’s first line of defense against germs
Sweat glands in it cool the body as sweat evaporates
Makes vitamin D when ultraviolet (UVB) sunlight hits it
Most cells of its outer layer are keratinocytes, which fill with the tough protein keratin
Melanocytes make melanin; people of all colorings have similar numbers of them but make different amounts of pigment
Its outermost layer, the stratum corneum, is made of flat, dead cells that are constantly shed
The dermis gets strength and stretch from collagen and elastin fibers
Tiny arrector pili muscles pull hairs upright, causing goosebumps
Sebaceous glands release oily sebum into hair follicles
Its ridges on the fingertips form fingerprints, which are unique to each person
Its outer layer has up to five strata: corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, and basale (“Come, Let’s Get Sun Burned”)
The stratum lucidum appears only in the thick parts on the palms and soles
Langerhans cells in its outer layer are lookouts for the immune system; that layer has no blood vessels
Merkel cells and Meissner’s corpuscles sense light touch; onion-like Pacinian corpuscles sense pressure and vibration
Langer’s lines follow the direction of its collagen fibers; surgeons cut along them to reduce scarring
Eccrine sweat glands cover most of the body; apocrine glands open into hair follicles in places like the armpits
UVB light turns 7-dehydrocholesterol in it into vitamin D3
Melanin comes in two main forms: brown-black eumelanin and red-yellow pheomelanin
Doctors estimate burned areas with the “rule of nines”; first-degree burns affect only the outer layer
Lungless salamanders breathe entirely through it and the lining of their mouths
A polar bear’s is black under its white-looking fur
Snakes shed the outer layer of theirs, often in one piece, in a process called ecdysis
Francis Galton sorted fingerprints into arches, loops, and whorls; koala fingerprints look very similar to ours
Greek “derma” and Latin “cutis” name it, giving us “dermatology” and “subcutaneous”

trap.title: The organ, or one layer?
trap.body: Because this organ includes the epidermis, many clues describe only the outer layer: its strata, keratinocytes, melanocytes, and Langerhans cells. Quiz bowl also has tossups that want the epidermis itself, and on those, “skin” is too general. Tossups on the whole organ, in turn, only prompt on “epidermis” or “dermis.”
trap.fix: Listen to the noun. “This organ” or “this largest organ” means skin; “this layer” or “this outermost layer” means epidermis; “this layer beneath the epidermis,” with collagen and sweat glands, means dermis.
trap.line: Real answer line: Skin (accept integument; prompt on epidermis, dermis, or integumentary system)

topics.name: Sleep
topics.kicker: Nightly resting state of brain and body · Cycles through REM and non-REM
topics.dates: Takes up about a third of a human life
topics.briefing: You will spend about a third of your life asleep, and your brain stays busy the whole time. Each night it cycles through light and deep non-REM stages and REM sleep, when the eyes dart around and most vivid dreams happen, roughly every 90 minutes. Scientists think sleep helps the brain store memories and clear out waste, and experts say kids 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours a night and teens need 8 to 10.
topics.answerHtml: Sleep (accept sleeping or specific stages such as REM sleep; prompt on REM alone; do not accept “dreaming” or “hibernation”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: By recording eye movements at night, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman discovered a stage of this state in 1953 at the University of Chicago. During that stage, the eyes dart back and forth beneath closed lids.
tossups.r: That stage, called REM, is when most vivid dreams happen. For 10 points, name this nightly resting state.

tossups.p: In 1938, Nathaniel Kleitman and a colleague spent 32 days deep in Kentucky’s Mammoth Cave, trying to switch their daily cycle of waking and this state to a 28-hour schedule. Kleitman is often called the father of modern research on this state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state that the body’s circadian rhythm helps time each night.

tossups.p: Bursts of brain waves called spindles and sudden large waves called K-complexes mark the second stage of this state, known as N2. Overnight tests called polysomnography [“pol-ee-som-NOG-ruh-fee”] record brain waves, eye movements, and muscle activity during this state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, which includes REM and non-REM stages and usually happens at night.

tossups.p: Growth hormone is released mainly during the deepest stage of this state, when slow, tall delta waves appear on an EEG. Somnambulism [“som-NAM-byuh-liz-um”] and night terrors usually happen during that deep stage, which is called N3.
tossups.r: People are hardest to wake during that stage. For 10 points, name this nightly state that includes REM and non-REM stages.

tossups.p: French scientist Michel Jouvet [“zhoo-VAY”] called one stage of this state “paradoxical,” because the brain is nearly as active as when awake while most muscles go limp. That loss of muscle tone, called atonia, keeps people from acting out their dreams.
tossups.r: People spend about a third of their lives in this state. For 10 points, name this state that people normally enter at night.

tossups.p: Studies of Doberman dogs helped show that a lack of signaling by the brain chemical orexin, also called hypocretin, can cause narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy can drop into this state suddenly during the day, and many also have cataplexy, a sudden muscle weakness set off by strong emotions.
tossups.r: It cycles through several stages, including REM. For 10 points, name this state that people usually enter each night.

tossups.p: Alexander Borbély’s two-process model says this state is controlled by a circadian clock and by a pressure that builds the longer a person stays awake. A molecule called adenosine builds up in the brain while a person is awake, and caffeine blocks its receptors.
tossups.r: Experts recommend that teenagers get 8 to 10 hours of it each night. For 10 points, name this state that people enter when they go to bed.

tossups.p: The suprachiasmatic [“soo-pruh-kye-az-MAT-ik”] nucleus in the hypothalamus acts as a master clock for this state, using signals from light-sensing cells in the retina. In darkness, the pineal gland releases melatonin to help bring on this state.
tossups.r: Its stages include N1, N2, N3, and REM. For 10 points, name this nightly state.

tossups.p: Dolphins can let one half of the brain enter this state while the other half stays alert, which lets them keep surfacing to breathe. Some birds do the same “unihemispheric” trick, keeping one eye open to watch for predators.
tossups.r: In humans, it includes REM and non-REM stages. For 10 points, name this state that people need every night.

tossups.p: A 2013 study of mice found that the brain’s glymphatic [“glim-FAT-ik”] system, which flushes out waste with cerebrospinal fluid, works much faster during this state. Scientists also think this state helps the brain store new memories.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state that experts say kids aged 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours of each night.

tossups.p: The Greek god Hypnos, the twin brother of Thanatos [“THAN-uh-tohs”], personified this state, and his Roman counterpart was Somnus, whose name gives us the word “insomnia.” In Ovid’s _Metamorphoses_, Morpheus, a son of Somnus, brings dreams to people in this state.
tossups.r: The hormone melatonin helps bring on this state. For 10 points, name this nightly resting state.

tossups.p: A hypnic jerk is a sudden twitch of the muscles that can jolt people just as they drift into this state. The drowsy in-between period as a person drifts into this state is called the hypnagogic [“hip-nuh-GOJ-ik”] state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, which cycles through REM and non-REM stages about every 90 minutes.

tossups.p: People with obstructive apnea stop breathing for short periods during this state, and many use a CPAP machine to keep the airway open. Insomnia is a disorder in which people struggle to get into or stay in this state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state that people typically enter at bedtime and leave when they wake up.

tossups.p: Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in 1924 and described alpha waves, which appear when a person is awake but relaxed with closed eyes. As a person drifts into this state, those waves give way to slower theta waves.
tossups.r: Going without enough of it makes people tired and less focused. For 10 points, name this state that people normally enter every night.

tossups.p: Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young shared a 2017 Nobel Prize for showing how a gene called “period” helps run the circadian clock in fruit flies. A similar internal clock in people helps time this state, so jet lag can throw it off schedule.
tossups.r: Most vivid dreams happen during its REM stage. For 10 points, name this nightly state of rest.

clues.t: Divided into REM (rapid eye movement) and non-REM stages
Most vivid dreams happen during its REM stage
The pineal gland releases the hormone melatonin in darkness to help bring it on
People spend about a third of their lives in this state
Timed by the body’s roughly 24-hour internal clock, the circadian rhythm
Cycles through its stages about every 90 minutes, several times a night
Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman discovered REM in 1953 at the University of Chicago
Studied overnight with polysomnography, which records brain waves (EEG), eye movements, and muscle activity
Its deepest stage, N3 (slow-wave), shows slow delta waves and is the hardest to wake from
During REM, most muscles are temporarily paralyzed (atonia), so people don’t act out their dreams
The suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus is the master clock that times it
Adenosine builds up while a person is awake, creating pressure for it; caffeine blocks adenosine receptors
Disorders include insomnia (trouble getting or staying in it) and obstructive apnea, often treated with a CPAP machine
Experts recommend 9 to 12 hours a night for kids 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teens
Stage N2 shows bursts called spindles and large waves called K-complexes
Michel Jouvet called REM “paradoxical” because the brain is nearly as active as when awake
A lack of orexin (hypocretin) signaling can cause narcolepsy, often with cataplexy, a sudden muscle weakness
Narcoleptic Doberman dogs helped researchers find an orexin receptor gene
Dolphins and some birds rest one half of the brain at a time (“unihemispheric”), keeping one eye open
Nathaniel Kleitman spent 32 days in Kentucky’s Mammoth Cave in 1938 testing a 28-hour day
A 2013 mouse study found that the brain’s glymphatic system clears waste faster during it
Growth hormone is released mostly during its deepest, slow-wave stage
Personified by the Greek god Hypnos (Roman Somnus), twin of Thanatos; in Ovid, Somnus’s son Morpheus brings dreams
A hypnic jerk is a sudden twitch while drifting off; the drowsy in-between period is called hypnagogic
Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in 1924 and described alpha waves, seen in relaxed, awake people
Alexander Borbély’s two-process model: a pressure that builds while awake, plus the circadian clock
Hall, Rosbash, and Young shared a 2017 Nobel Prize for the “period” gene and other parts of the fruit fly’s circadian clock
Somnambulism and night terrors usually happen during its deep N3 stage

trap.title: Sleep, dreams, or hibernation?
trap.body: Sleep tossups lean hard on REM clues, so players blurt “dreams” or just “REM,” but dreaming is something that happens during sleep, and “REM” by itself earns only a prompt here. Other near-misses name what controls sleep (melatonin, the circadian rhythm) or a disorder (insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnea). Hibernation and torpor are energy-saving states that are different from true sleep.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this state” with stages N1, N2, N3, and REM, say sleep. Save “circadian rhythm” for questions about the 24-hour clock itself, and “melatonin” for questions asking for a hormone.
trap.line: Real answer line: Sleep (accept sleeping or specific stages such as REM sleep; prompt on REM alone; do not accept “dreaming” or “hibernation”)

topics.name: X chromosome
topics.kicker: Sex chromosome · Two copies in most females, one in most males
topics.dates: First spotted by Hermann Henking in 1891
topics.briefing: Most human females have two X chromosomes, and most males have one X paired with a much smaller Y. Because males have only one copy, recessive traits carried on the X, like red-green color blindness and hemophilia, show up far more often in boys. In females, one X in each cell is switched off, which is why calico cats, whose fur-color gene rides on the X, are almost always female.
topics.answerHtml: X chromosome (accept X; prompt on sex chromosome or chromosome; do not accept “Y chromosome”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Hermann Henking gave this chromosome its one-letter name after spotting it in the cells of firebugs in 1891, and Clarence McClung later suggested that this “accessory chromosome” helps determine sex. Nettie Stevens backed up that idea in 1905 by studying mealworms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sex chromosome, of which human females usually have two copies.

tossups.p: In 1913, Alfred Sturtevant made the first genetic map using genes on this chromosome in fruit flies. Sturtevant’s teacher, Thomas Hunt Morgan, had shown in 1910 that a white-eyed male fly carried its eye-color gene on this chromosome.
tossups.r: Human females usually have two copies of it. For 10 points, name this chromosome that human males inherit from their mothers.

tossups.p: Mary Lyon proposed in 1961 that in the cells of female mammals like mice and humans, one copy of this chromosome is randomly shut down. The inactive copy condenses into a dark spot that Murray Barr and Ewart Bertram first saw in cat nerve cells in 1949.
tossups.r: That spot is called a Barr body. For 10 points, name this sex chromosome found in two copies in most human females.

tossups.p: A long noncoding RNA made from a gene on this chromosome coats one copy of it and silences most of its genes. That process, called dosage compensation, keeps female mammals from making twice as much of this chromosome’s gene products as males do.
tossups.r: Females usually have two copies of it. For 10 points, name this sex chromosome whose partner in males is the Y.

tossups.p: Calico and tortoiseshell cats are almost always female, because a gene for orange or black fur sits on this chromosome and one copy is randomly shut off in each cell, leaving patches. The rare male calico usually has two copies of this chromosome plus a Y.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this chromosome, which also carries genes linked to red-green color blindness and hemophilia.

tossups.p: A syndrome named for a “fragile” site on this chromosome is caused by too many repeats of the DNA triplet CGG in a gene called FMR1. That syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability.
tossups.r: Most human males have one copy of it. For 10 points, name this sex chromosome, which pairs with the Y.

tossups.p: The largest known human gene, which codes for the muscle protein dystrophin, is found on this chromosome. Changes in that gene cause Duchenne [“doo-SHEN”] muscular dystrophy, which mostly affects boys because they usually have only one copy of this chromosome.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sex chromosome, two copies of which are found in most human females.

tossups.p: Queen Victoria passed a gene variant on this chromosome to several European royal families, and her great-grandson Alexei, heir to Russia’s throne, inherited the clotting disorder it causes. That disorder, hemophilia, is far more common in males.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sex chromosome that pairs with a Y in most males.

tossups.p: In 1794, John Dalton described his own color blindness, and in 1995 scientists tested DNA from his preserved eye and found that he lacked a working gene for a green-sensing pigment, which is carried on this chromosome.
tossups.r: Because males have only one copy of this chromosome, red-green color blindness is far more common in them. For 10 points, name this sex chromosome.

tossups.p: People with Klinefelter syndrome have two copies of this chromosome plus a Y, so their cells contain one Barr body. People with Turner syndrome have just one copy of this chromosome and no second sex chromosome at all.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sex chromosome, which human females usually inherit from both parents.

tossups.p: Small pseudoautosomal [“SOO-doh-aw-tuh-SOH-mul”] regions at the tips of this chromosome let it pair up and swap DNA with its much smaller partner during meiosis in males. Males are hemizygous for most genes on this chromosome, since they usually have only one copy.
tossups.r: That smaller partner is the Y chromosome. For 10 points, name this sex chromosome, of which most females have two.

tossups.p: Male platypuses have five different versions of this chromosome along with five different Y chromosomes. Birds do not have this chromosome at all; instead, female birds have one Z chromosome and one W chromosome.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mammalian sex chromosome, of which human females usually have two copies.

tossups.p: In fruit flies, sex depends on the ratio of copies of this chromosome to sets of other chromosomes, and males make up for having just one copy by roughly doubling its activity. Human females instead silence one of their two copies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sex chromosome, which human males inherit only from their mothers.

tossups.p: In 2020, this became the first human chromosome to be sequenced completely, from one end to the other, with no gaps. It carries the gene for G6PD, an enzyme whose shortage can cause anemia after a person eats fava beans.
tossups.r: It is much larger than its partner, the Y. For 10 points, name this chromosome found in two copies in most human females.

tossups.p: A father passes his copy of this chromosome to all of his daughters and none of his sons. Because sons get their only copy from their mothers, a son who inherits a recessive allele on it will usually show that trait.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sex chromosome that pairs with a Y in most human males.

clues.t: One of the two human sex chromosomes; its partner, the Y, is much smaller
Human females usually have two copies; males usually have one, paired with a Y
A male inherits his only copy from his mother
Carries genes linked to red-green color blindness, which is far more common in males
Carries a gene linked to hemophilia, a clotting disorder far more common in males
Thomas Hunt Morgan’s white-eyed fruit fly (1910) showed that a gene was carried on it
In female mammals, one copy in each cell is shut down and condensed into a Barr body
Calico and tortoiseshell cats are almost always female because a fur-color gene sits on it
People with Turner syndrome have only one copy and no second sex chromosome
People with Klinefelter syndrome have two copies plus a Y
A father passes his copy to all of his daughters and none of his sons
Males are “hemizygous” for most of its genes, so a single recessive allele shows up in them
First spotted by Hermann Henking in 1891, in the cells of firebugs; he gave it its one-letter name
Clarence McClung linked this “accessory chromosome” to sex; Nettie Stevens backed him up by studying mealworms (1905)
Alfred Sturtevant made the first genetic map in 1913 from fruit fly genes on it
Mary Lyon proposed random shut-off in 1961 (“lyonization”); Murray Barr and Ewart Bertram had found the Barr body in cat nerve cells in 1949
A long noncoding RNA coats the copy that gets silenced; this dosage compensation evens out gene activity
A syndrome named for a “fragile” site on it, caused by repeated CGG triplets in FMR1, is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability
Holds the dystrophin gene, the largest known human gene; changes in it cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy
John Dalton described his own color blindness in 1794; DNA from his preserved eye was tested in 1995
Queen Victoria’s great-grandson Alexei, heir to Russia’s throne, inherited hemophilia
Pseudoautosomal regions at its tips pair and swap DNA with the Y during meiosis in males
Male platypuses have five different versions of it (and five Y’s); birds use Z and W chromosomes instead
In fruit flies, sex depends on the ratio of its copies to sets of other chromosomes

trap.title: X, Y, or just chromosome?
trap.body: Tossups on this chromosome are full of clues about sex chromosomes, Barr bodies, and the Y, so players blurt “Y chromosome,” “sex chromosome,” or just “chromosome.” The two sex chromosomes are very different: the Y is small, carries far fewer genes, and passes only from father to son.
trap.fix: Calico cats, Barr bodies, lyonization, hemophilia, color blindness, fragile X syndrome, or “two copies in females” mean the X chromosome. Father-to-son inheritance means the Y. Saying only “sex chromosome” or “chromosome” earns a prompt, so be ready to add the letter.
trap.line: Real answer line: X chromosome (accept X; prompt on sex chromosome or chromosome; do not accept “Y chromosome”)
